[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Tutorial: Mixed Precision Training with PyTorch (AMP, float16, and bfloat16)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mixed precision training combines single-precision (FP32) and lower-precision formats (FP16 or BF16) to reduce memory consumption and accelerate training times on modern GPUs. In this tutorial, we will explore Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in PyTorch."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Understanding FP16 vs BF16"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP16 (Half Precision): Offers a wide dynamic range but requires loss scaling to prevent gradient underflow due to its limited exponent bits."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"BF16 (Brain Floating Point): Shares the same exponent range as FP32, making it much more stable for deep learning without the strict need for gradient scaling."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Setting up Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"PyTorch provides the torch.cuda.amp module to automatically cast operations to lower precision where safe, while keeping critical operations in FP32 for numerical stability."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Initialize model, optimizer, and scaler
model = MyModel().cuda()
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. The Training Loop with GradScaler"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"When using FP16, gradients can become too small to represent. GradScaler multiplies the loss by a scaling factor before the backward pass to prevent underflow."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"for inputs, targets in dataloader:
    inputs, targets = inputs.cuda(), targets.cuda()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Forward pass with autocast
    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.float16):
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets)

    # Scaled backward pass and optimizer step
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Using bfloat16 for Simplicity"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"If your hardware supports bfloat16 (such as NVIDIA Ampere architectures or newer), you can bypass the GradScaler entirely because of BF16's larger dynamic range."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# No GradScaler required for bfloat16
with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    outputs = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets)

loss.backward()
optimizer.step()"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"By incorporating AMP into your PyTorch training pipelines, you can drastically decrease memory footprints and increase throughput with minimal code changes."}]
